newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl under pressure for results in tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl under pressure for results in tax talks.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl came under pressure on Monday to get results at tax reform talks with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) which resume after weeks of sniping on Tuesday.

Kohl has sought to inject new urgency into his government's drive to reform tax, pensions and health policy since he announced recently that he would seek election for a record fifth term of office in autumn 1998.

His three-party coalition agreed on Sunday to adopt a plan which would put state pensions on a gradual downward glide path and contain costs which would otherwise explode due to the "greying" of Germany's 80 million population.

But the real test comes on Tuesday when Kohl leads a team into crunch talks with SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine which could determine whether a deal can be struck or whether tax reforms could founder on the SPD's majority in the upper house of parliament.

After over a month of delay in negotiations, sparked first by a row over coal subsidies and then prolonged by deep doubts among SPD leaders over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's fiscal arithmetic, business leaders urged quick action.

"Implementing the tax reform is of huge importance for the creation of new jobs and keeping existing ones, and as a signal to both German and foreign investors," said Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the BDI German industry federation.
"If it fails, German investors will flee the country. Foreign investors will avoid it even more than before -- with catastrophic results for the jobs market."

Franz Schoser, chief executive of the DIHT chambers of industry and commerce, echoed Henkel's view, saying: "We must carry out these reforms as quickly as possible and look to other countries which have already gone down this path."
Waigel has proposed a package of corporate and income tax cuts worth a net 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion) designed to stimulate investment and put Germany's 4.5 million jobless back to work.
The SPD has negotiated on an 'a la carte' basis -- accepting what it likes, rejecting what it doesn't and tossing in extra demands of its own apparently at will.

To secure his backing for the tax reforms, Lafontaine wants a 30 billion mark cut in Germany's high labour insurance costs by July, higher child benefits and tax allowances and a cut next year in income tax for ordinary wage earners.

He also wants Waigel to demonstrate how he can plug a budget gap of over 50 billion marks that Lafontaine says will be caused by the tax reforms -- risking Germany's ability to cut borrowing and lead European monetary union from the front.

Coalition sources said on Monday the government could go along with a smaller reduction in the so-called non-wage costs of 15 billion marks -- equal to a one-point hike in value-added tax or an extra 12 pfennigs in tax on a litre of petrol. But compliance would depend on SPD flexibility in other areas.
Lafontaine on Sunday called for a breakthrough in the talks but Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said his expectations were limited.

"If the SPD follows Oskar Lafontaine, who is opening a new debate about redistributing wealth by calling for a rise in child benefits, then that is not a good way to go about creating jobs," Schaeuble said in Berlin.

Despite Kohl's appeals to maintain a cross-party consensus on pensions, the SPD said it would oppose coalition plans to allow the payout on compulsory state pensions to fall to 64 percent of average net wages by 2015 from 70 percent now.
SPD social affairs spokesman Rudolf Dressler told the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung that allowing pensions to fall that far would push millions of Germans into poverty.

"If the coalition is not prepared to give up on this point, then it must pass it alone through parliament and stand up for it at the 1998 elections," he told the paper. -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.721 German Marks)
